blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given three arrays, each sorted in ascending order. Return every value that appears in **all three**, without duplicates, in sorted order.

blocks.alt: Three sorted arrays. The values 20 and 80 appear in all three and are highlighted.

elements.text: Common Elements in Three Sorted Arrays
elements.originalText: Common Elements in Three Sorted Arrays

blocks.text: This is **Intersection of two arrays**, stretched to three. Because all three inputs are sorted, you shouldn't need a set or any extra memory — the sorted order carries the information.
For each value of `a`, check whether it's in `b` and in `c`.
Each check scans a whole array, so this is **O(n1 × (n2 + n3))**. Using binary search for the checks improves it to O(n1 log n2 + n1 log n3), but we can do better still.
The key insight: always advance the smallest
Keep one pointer per array. Look at the three front values:

items: If all three are **equal**, that value is common: record it and move all three pointers.

Otherwise, find the **smallest** of the three. That value can't be common: at least one other array's front is already bigger, and since that array is sorted, it will never go back down to it. So move the pointer on the smallest value (on every array where it appears).

blocks.text: Every step moves at least one pointer forward, and pointers never move back, so the total work is the combined length of the arrays.

blocks.alt: One step of the three-pointer walk: fronts are 1, 6 and 3. The smallest, 1, cannot be common, so pointer i moves forward.

blocks.text: Watch which pointers move on each step. With repeated values, notice how a value already recorded isn't recorded again.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n1 × (n2 + n3)) time. Three pointers: O(n1 + n2 + n3) time and O(1) extra space.

blocks.text: Every step moves at least one pointer, and there are n1 + n2 + n3 steps at most: **O(n1 + n2 + n3) time, O(1) extra space** besides the answer.

items: **Nothing common** — the loop ends when any array runs out, returning `[]`.
**One array empty** — the answer is immediately empty.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

"Advance the pointer that is furthest behind" generalises to **k** sorted lists: finding the smallest range that covers one number from each list, or merging k sorted lists, both keep the fronts in a heap so the smallest is always one step away.
